newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: AIDS boy fights to go to South African school.
newsitem.headline: AIDS boy fights to go to South African school.

text.p: Parents sought on Monday to bar an eight-year-old boy with AIDS from their children's school, the first time South Africa has grappled publicly with the issue.

Some parents at the primary school in a trendy middle-class Johannesburg suburb vowed to wrap their children in protective plastic clothing if Nkosi Johnson was admitted. Parents said they did not want their children exposed to the risk of contracting AIDS.
"We have been waiting for something like this to happen. It is the result of fear and of ignorance," said Christopher Payne of the National Association of People with HIV and AIDS.

The boy's mother and AIDS activists say risks are tiny if precautions are taken, such as using bleach to kill the HIV virus -- which leads to AIDS -- in any blood spill, and the school has no legal right to bar the boy.
School governors and local education authorities have yet to pronounce on the case, the first to make national headlines even though AIDS is rampant in South Africa.

Newspapers said Johnson is believed to be the oldest surviving child with AIDS in South Africa, where estimates put the number of people with the disease at four percent of the population, or some one and a half million people.

Payne said South African parents usually were too scared to admit their children had the illness and covered it up for fear of ostracism, especially in the black community. In rural areas, where education is basic, many children with the virus are simply kept away from school.
"There are thousands of HIV positive kids at school, but I don't know of any cases where they are open about it," he said.
Some callers to a Johannesburg radio chat show on Monday said children with AIDS should be segregated in special schools, or be forced to wear bracelets to distinguish them.

AIDS is crippling sub-Saharan Africa, where it is spread largely by unprotected heterosexual intercourse. Promiscuity is common and resistance to using condoms strong. As a result many babies are born with the virus and later contract AIDS (Acquired Immune Deficiency Syndrome).
Similar battles have been fought in many countries where authorities have ruled that children with AIDS have a right to education in normal schools.
